text: The evidence is other people's pictures: murals, engravings, footage shot for other reasons. Sylvia Morales runs twenty-three minutes from Aztec society through the independence fighting of 1810, the labor strikes of 1872, the revolution of 1910, and the organizing of her own decade, and the compression is the point — a chronology this long, cut this tight, makes recurrence visible where a longer film would only make episodes. Women appear as workers first. Poor, unnamed in the record, and consistently at the front of a strike or a march, which the film demonstrates by returning to the same kind of image across two centuries and two countries. The National Film Registry took it in, a short made outside any studio, whose method is to look again at pictures already in circulation.

Silent, sixteen millimetre, twenty-one minutes, no commentary of any kind. What the camera finds is the ground at Falkenau, in Czechoslovakia, where Allied forces reached a Nazi concentration camp as the war in Europe ended, and then the burial of the dead they found there. Without narration the film has one instrument only: where the operator chooses to stand, and how long he lets a shot run. It is enough. Samuel Fuller's name on the reel is the reason anyone went looking for it, and the National Film Registry is why it can still be seen; neither fact prepares a viewer for much. This is not a report and does not argue. Someone with a small camera decided the dead should be seen being put into the earth by the living, in daylight, at the speed it actually took.

A patient who cannot speak is given a voice-over, and the training film she is inside stops behaving like a training film. Naomi Feil was a social worker whose work was with language-impaired patients; here she is in front of the camera as a nurse and behind it as co-director, in twenty-four minutes made for classrooms of caregivers. The device is plain and hard to sit with: while the people at the bedside read a face and guess, the soundtrack carries the sentences the injury has sealed off. Frustration, in full grammar. She and her husband Edward Feil made dozens of these; this one took CINE's Golden Eagle, and decades on it is still booked by artists and independent filmmakers with no interest in the curriculum. What lasts is the ordinary awfulness of being addressed as though absent.

The job is carrying the mail, which in a mountain village means a fixed route and unavoidable meetings with whoever lives along it. David Kinemon is good-natured and in no hurry to be anything else; he takes the round because his brother cannot, and the Hatburn brothers are on that road. Columbia released this in 1930 as a talking version of a silent picture from 1921 that audiences still remembered, which puts John G. Blystone in a strange spot: sixty-five minutes to re-earn a story people could recite, with the rural quiet now audible. The National Board of Review put it among the year's ten best. What holds the middle together is errand and obligation — porches, a family's arithmetic about who can be spared — and the fact that the route has to be walked again tomorrow.

Every Wednesday at noon the same women stand in the same place and ask the Japanese government for an apology. Byun Young-joo builds ninety-three minutes around that repetition, then follows the women home. They were taken by the Japanese army during the imperial years and held for sex, and the silence afterward was not theirs; it was arranged, and they were expected to keep it out of shame. The documentary's method is duration. Stay long enough and a demonstrator becomes a woman with a kitchen, a temper, an aching body, opinions about her neighbours — precisely the shift that official language has spent fifty years preventing. The Korean Film Archive counts it among a hundred national films. It is filmed close, at their pace, and it never once explains them to a stranger.

Dance was the connective tissue of Yupik life: between the living and the dead, between inherited knowledge and new, between what a person can do and what the unseen can. Sarah Elder's film gives that ninety minutes, at the tempo of the events rather than the tempo of an explanation. Ethnographic footage usually arrives pre-chewed, a voice telling the viewer what has just been seen; the choice here is closer to attendance, songs allowed their full length, the drumming left to establish its own duration. Length is the argument. An evening that took an evening cannot be quoted in ninety seconds without turning into costume. The National Film Registry holds it, which for a documentary this local means somebody decided the record itself, unshortened, was the thing worth keeping.

A jazz musician keeps declining to commit to an art student, and the film declines to make a plot of it: twelve minutes of vignettes, black and white, 1965. Ray Manzarek shot it as a UCLA student, with Dorothy Fujikawa — later his wife of forty years — opposite Henry Crismonde. The Sunset Strip is here, the Whiskey A Go Go among the locations, and Jim Morrison appears briefly, some way from any stage. Impressionism suits the subject: a man avoiding a decision produces recurrences rather than scenes, and twelve minutes is exactly as long as that can hold. The National Film Registry took it in 2021, an odd fate for a student exercise and a fair one, since what the film keeps is a handful of Los Angeles rooms on the afternoons somebody carried a camera into them.

The people on the sidewalk look straight into the lens, and none of them has been caught unawares. H. Lee Waters filmed a North Carolina town in 1941 and called the series Movies of Local People, a title that puts the town on both sides of the camera; nobody here is a subject in the usual documentary sense. Two hours and seventeen minutes, silent, without a story. What accumulates instead is behaviour under observation: a wave, a stiffened shoulder, a boy checking whether he is in it, hundreds of small negotiations with a machine that has come to town. The length matters, since the interest lies not in any one face but in the sheer number of them, gathered in a single place in a single year. The National Film Registry keeps the reels.

The footage was commissioned to be shown in a Philadelphia department store. That errand is inseparable from what happens in front of the camera at Crow Agency in 1908: Rodman Wanamaker paid, Joseph K. Dixon and his son Roland shot, and both men had decided in advance that they were recording a 'vanishing race' — a conclusion the people being filmed were not asked to confirm. Forty-three minutes survive, the only film known from the expedition, and they hold Crow Fair, ordinary business on the agency, and a staged Battle of Little Big Horn with four men who had scouted for Custer taking part. The restaging is the strangest stretch. What the National Film Registry preserves is therefore double: a community going about its year, and the theory of extinction that sent a camera to watch it.

A factory stands where a village used to be, and it is empty. The man looking for the village has spent years in an asylum, so his memory of the place is already the least trusted account available. Now the landscape has sided with his doctors. Bae Yong-kyun spends a hundred and eleven minutes here, which indicates the kind of film it is: not an inquiry with an answer at the end but a long passage across ground that has been overwritten. The premise is nearly a joke about the speed of industrialisation — the plant arrives, the village it replaced leaves no forwarding address — except that nobody inside the film is placed to laugh. A man without a village has no relatives to be ashamed of him and no work to be given. The Korean Film Archive counts it among a hundred.

Pancho Villa's life arrives secondhand, cut together with scissors from films and newsreels that had entirely other jobs to do. Edmundo Padilla drew on decades of Mexican and American silent production, setting staged battle against actuality until a biography emerges from footage nobody shot for the purpose — some of it shot to make the opposite case. Sixty minutes, mostly combat: crowds, cavalry, smoke, all of it borrowed. The interest is in the direction of the retelling. Villa had been on American screens for years, arranged by other hands for other rooms; here the same reels are recut so that he comes out a hero, which turns the ownership of an image into a matter of splicing. The National Film Registry preserves the result, an argument assembled from other people's footage.

A drink after work, and a new man on the forging team whom the others have taken out because that is what is done. Ju Wan-ik joins two hundred people at the Dongseong Metalworks, all of them poor in the specific way a wage can make a person poor, and for a long stretch the film attends to that — shifts, heat, the etiquette by which exhausted men make room for one more. The title says where this ends up. The hundred and five minutes are spent on the distance to it, on how slowly a workplace turns into a position somebody is willing to hold. Made in 1990, filmed on a floor the camera seems to know its way around. The Korean Film Archive keeps it among a hundred national titles.

Sumatra, a village at the forest edge, a father and a son who hunt: in 1931 that was armature enough for a feature. Ernest B. Schoedsack fits sixty-six minutes of story to Ali and Bin, and to whatever the jungle would consent to do in front of a lens, which lands the picture in the middle ground the period was fond of — animals and weather behaving as they do, people directed to behave as though unobserved. The hunting is both the plot and the reason for the trip. The National Board of Review named it one of the year's ten best, when audiences would sit an hour for footage of somewhere far off and call it adventure. The unease now comes from the same place as the pleasure: the material was never fabricated, and the people in it were material too.

An office, 1919, and one new employee whose arrival ends the productivity of every man in the room. The comedy is spatial: desks in rows, sightlines, the arithmetic of who can see whom, and a young woman who grasps that being looked at is a form of leverage available to someone hired at the bottom. Fifty minutes, briskly turned. The joke sits exactly where 1919 wanted it — a vamp by reputation, virtuous in conduct, and the film has that both ways as long as it can manage. She sets her sights on the one man who has not noticed her, which is the oldest engine in romance and here doubles as a remark about the office itself: attention is the currency, and he is the only one not spending it. It is on the National Film Registry.
